q: Magnetism is a phenomenon associated with _____.
e: Magnetism is defined as a phenomenon associated with a magnetic field, which surrounds any magnet.

q: A magnet has a _____ around it.
e: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where its magnetic force and effects can be detected.

q: Magnets are materials which exhibit magnetic properties such as attracting magnetic materials, having two poles, and _____.
a: like poles attract, unlike poles repel
like poles repel, unlike poles attract
e: The fundamental law of magnetic poles states that like poles repel each other, while unlike poles attract.

q: Magnetite consists of an oxide of _____.
e: Magnetite is a natural magnet that primarily consists of an oxide of iron.

q: Materials such as cobalt, nickel, and some alloys such as steel are called _____.
e: Materials that are attracted by a magnet, such as cobalt, nickel, and steel, are classified as magnetic materials.

q: Materials such as brass, copper, wood, and plastics that are not attracted by a magnet are called _____.
e: Materials that show no attraction to a magnet are classified as non-magnetic materials.

q: Any material that is able to keep its magnetism for a long time is called a _____.
e: A permanent magnet is defined as any material that retains its magnetism for a long period of time.

q: Modern-day permanent magnets are usually made of steel and special alloys such as alcomax and _____.
e: Special alloys used for modern permanent magnets include alcomax and alnico.

q: Alcomax and alnico contain metals such as iron, nickel, copper, cobalt, and _____.
e: The composition of alcomax and alnico alloys includes iron, nickel, copper, cobalt, and aluminium.

q: Ceramic magnet is made from powders called _____.
e: Ceramic magnets are manufactured from powders known as ferrites.

q: Ferrites are compounds of iron oxide with _____.
e: Ferrites are specifically defined as compounds of iron oxide combined with other metal oxides.

q: Ceramic magnets are known to be _____.
e: A notable physical property of ceramic magnets is that they are brittle.

q: The two ends of the magnet where most steel pins are attracted are called the _____ of the magnet.
e: The regions of a magnet where the magnetic force is strongest and attracts the most pins are called the poles.

q: When a suspended bar magnet comes to rest, one end always points towards the northern end of the Earth. This end is called the _____.
e: The end of a freely suspended magnet that points towards the Earth's geographic north is the north-seeking pole.

q: The north-seeking pole and south-seeking pole of the magnet are usually referred to as simply the north pole ($N$-pole) and the _____.
e: The south-seeking pole is conventionally abbreviated and referred to as the south pole ($S$-pole).

q: According to the law of magnetic poles, like poles _____ and unlike poles attract.
e: The fundamental law of magnetism dictates that like magnetic poles repel each other.

q: A magnet can be used as a _____ for navigation.
e: Due to its north-seeking property, a magnet is the core component of a navigational compass.

q: Magnetic pole strength is a measure of the _____ of magnetic poles.
e: Magnetic pole strength quantifies the intensity or strength of the magnetic poles.

q: The force between two poles is directly proportional to the product of the pole strengths and _____ proportional to the distance squared between them.
e: Magnetic force follows an inverse-square law with respect to the distance between the poles.

q: When a magnetised steel bar is cut into smaller pieces, every piece is a magnet with a(n) _____ and $S$-pole.
e: Cutting a magnet always results in smaller pieces that each possess both an $N$-pole and an $S$-pole.

q: A magnetised bar is composed of tiny magnets all lined up with their $N$-poles pointing in the _____.
e: Magnetisation occurs when the magnetic domains (tiny magnets) align in the same direction.

q: In an unmagnetised bar, the 'tiny' magnets point in a _____ direction.
e: In an unmagnetised state, the magnetic domains are oriented randomly, canceling out the overall magnetic effect.

q: In an unmagnetised bar, the resulting magnetic effect of all the tiny magnets is _____ out.
e: The random orientation of domains in an unmagnetised bar causes their individual magnetic fields to cancel each other out.

q: The magnetic field is a region where _____ can be detected.
e: By definition, a magnetic field is the specific region in space where magnetic effects are observable.

q: Distribution of magnetic field can be visualized by the _____.
e: Magnetic lines of force are the conceptual tool used to visualize the distribution and pattern of a magnetic field.

q: The magnetic lines of force leave the _____ pole and enter the south pole.
e: By convention, magnetic lines of force are drawn emerging from the north pole and entering the south pole.

q: To show the pattern of a magnetic field around a bar magnet, we can sprinkle _____ lightly on a paper.
e: Iron filings are used because they are magnetic and will align themselves along the magnetic lines of force.

q: The Earth has a _____.
e: The Earth itself acts as a giant magnet, possessing its own global magnetic field.

q: We can think of the Earth as having an imaginary bar magnet inside it with magnetic north and _____ poles.
e: The Earth's magnetic field is modeled as an imaginary bar magnet with distinct north and south magnetic poles.

q: The magnetic north lies somewhere in the sea in northern _____ but has been shifting slowly over the years.
e: The Earth's magnetic north pole is geographically located in the sea in northern Canada and shifts over time.

q: A magnetic field has neither a starting point nor an end point because magnets never have a _____.
e: Unlike electric charges, magnetic monopoles do not exist, meaning magnetic field lines always form continuous closed loops.

q: A process of making a magnetic material into a magnet is called _____.
e: Magnetisation is the specific term for the process of converting a magnetic material into a magnet.

q: Two types of magnetisation are magnetisation by stroking and magnetisation using _____.
e: The two primary methods of magnetisation are the mechanical stroking method and the electrical method using direct current.

q: The best way to make powerful magnets is to use the magnetic effect of an _____.
e: Passing an electric current through a solenoid is the most effective method for creating powerful magnets.

q: A steel bar placed inside a solenoid with direct current passed through it becomes a _____.
e: Steel retains its magnetism after the current is switched off, making it a permanent magnet.

q: If an iron bar is placed inside a solenoid with direct current, it becomes magnetised temporarily as a(n) _____.
e: Iron loses its magnetism quickly once the current stops, functioning as a temporary electromagnet.

q: The polarities of the magnet produced by a solenoid depend on the _____ of the electric current.
e: Reversing the direction of the direct current will reverse the $N$-pole and $S$-pole of the resulting magnet.

q: In magnetisation by stroking, the magnet must be lifted _____ above the bar between successive strokes.
e: Lifting the magnet high prevents the return stroke from demagnetising or reversing the alignment of the domains.

q: The end of the steel bar where the strokes finish always has the _____ polarity to that of the end of the stroking magnet in contact with it.
e: The finishing end of the bar acquires the opposite polarity of the stroking magnet's contact end due to magnetic induction.

q: When a piece of unmagnetised magnetic material is brought near to the pole of a permanent magnet, it is attracted and becomes a magnet itself. This is called _____.
e: Induced magnetism is the temporary magnetisation of a material caused by the proximity of a permanent magnet.

q: In induced magnetism, the north pole of the permanent magnet induces a(n) _____ in the near end of the soft iron.
e: Unlike poles attract, so the $N$-pole of the permanent magnet induces an opposite $S$-pole in the nearest end of the soft iron.

q: In induced magnetism, the far end of the soft iron becomes a(n) _____.
e: Since the near end becomes an $S$-pole, the conservation of magnetic dipoles dictates that the far end must become an $N$-pole.

q: Iron is an element while steel is an alloy comprised of iron and _____.
e: Steel is fundamentally an alloy made by combining the element iron with carbon.

q: Magnetic materials such as steel which are harder to magnetise but retain their magnetism longer are called _____ magnetic materials.
e: Hard magnetic materials are characterized by their difficulty to magnetise and their ability to retain magnetism permanently.

q: Magnetic materials such as iron or special alloys like mumetal alloy which are easier to magnetise but do not retain their magnetism very long are called _____ magnetic materials.
e: Soft magnetic materials are easily magnetised and demagnetised, making them unsuitable for permanent magnets.

q: Soft iron can be _____ magnetised and demagnetised.
e: A defining property of soft iron is that it requires very little effort to both magnetise and demagnetise.

q: Steel is hard to magnetise and _____ than iron.
e: Steel's hard magnetic nature means it resists both the initial magnetisation and subsequent demagnetisation processes.

q: Soft iron can be magnetised by a _____ magnetic field.
e: Due to its high permeability, soft iron requires only a weak magnetic field to become fully magnetised.

q: Steel requires a _____ magnetic field to magnetise.
e: Because it is a hard magnetic material, steel necessitates a strong magnetic field to align its domains.

q: Soft iron retains its magnetism _____.
e: Soft iron loses its magnetism almost immediately after the external magnetising field is removed.

q: Steel retains its magnetism _____.
e: Steel is used for permanent magnets because it successfully retains its magnetism over a long period.

q: Soft magnetic materials are used for transformers, electromagnets, magnetic shielding, electric bell, and _____.
e: The temporary magnetic properties of soft materials make them ideal for devices like magnetic relays that require rapid switching.

q: Magnetic shielding is used to store magnetically sensitive instruments such as _____.
e: Magnetic shielding protects delicate, magnetically sensitive instruments like mechanical watches from external magnetic fields.
